questions.stem: Evidence shows that life has existed on Earth for about how long?
options: About 3.5 billion years
About 350 million years
About 4.5 billion years
About 65 million years
questions.explanation: Microfossils and geochemical evidence show that life has existed for around 3.5 billion years and has diversified over that time. About 4.5 billion years is the age of the Earth itself, before life appeared.

questions.stem: Which two features are shared by all known living cells?
options: Nucleic acids as genetic material and a cell membrane
A membrane-bound nucleus and a set of mitochondria
A cell wall made of cellulose and a set of chloroplasts
Linear chromosomes and membrane-bound organelles
questions.explanation: All known life forms have nucleic acids (DNA, and RNA) carrying genetic information and a cell membrane separating the cell from its surroundings. A nucleus, mitochondria and linear chromosomes are found only in eukaryotic cells.

questions.stem: Fossil stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old are found in rocks in Western Australia. Why are they evidence of early life?
options: They contain fossil eukaryotic cells with clearly visible nuclei inside
They are layered structures built by mats of microorganisms trapping sediment
They contain the preserved bones of the very earliest known multicellular animals
They are layers of coal formed from the remains of the first land plants
questions.explanation: Stromatolites form when mats of microorganisms, such as cyanobacteria, trap and bind sediment in layers. Living examples still form today, so the ancient layered structures are good evidence of early microbial life. Animals and land plants appeared far later.

questions.stem: Carbon in some very old rocks has a higher proportion of carbon-12 than carbon from non-living sources. Why is this treated as geochemical evidence of early life?
options: Living organisms convert carbon-13 into carbon-12 during respiration
Living organisms take up the lighter carbon-12 in preference to carbon-13
Carbon-12 forms only when radioactive carbon-14 decays inside cells
Volcanoes release only carbon-13, so carbon-12 must come from fossils
questions.explanation: Processes such as photosynthesis take up the lighter isotope carbon-12 slightly more readily than carbon-13, so carbon from living things is enriched in carbon-12. Organisms cannot change one isotope into another, and carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14, not carbon-12.

questions.stem: Which property of phospholipids supports the idea that membranes could have formed spontaneously on the early Earth?
options: They catalyse the joining of amino acids into proteins inside the early cell
They dissolve completely in water, spreading evenly through the early oceans
In water they assemble into bilayers and enclosed vesicles without any enzymes
They can copy themselves exactly by base pairing, like strands of nucleic acid
questions.explanation: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails, so in water they arrange themselves into bilayers that can close into vesicles. This can happen without enzymes, which is why membranes may have formed spontaneously. Phospholipids do not store or copy genetic information.

questions.stem: What is a ribozyme?
options: A DNA sequence that codes for an enzyme
An RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst
A protein enzyme that breaks down RNA
A ribosome found only in prokaryotes
questions.explanation: A ribozyme is RNA that catalyses a chemical reaction, as an enzyme does. The joining of amino acids in a ribosome is catalysed by its rRNA, so the ribosome itself contains a ribozyme. Most enzymes are proteins, but ribozymes show RNA can also catalyse.

questions.stem: Why do many scientists propose that the first simple cells used RNA, rather than DNA, as their genetic information?
options: RNA is double stranded, so it can be copied more accurately than DNA
RNA contains the base thymine, which DNA lacks, so it codes more amino acids
RNA can carry genetic information and some RNA can catalyse reactions
RNA is a more stable molecule than DNA, so it lasted longer in early oceans
questions.explanation: RNA can store information in its base sequence, and ribozymes show it can also act as a catalyst, so one molecule could have both copied itself and carried out reactions before proteins and DNA. RNA is usually single stranded and less stable than DNA, and it contains uracil rather than thymine.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the idea that prokaryotic cells existed before eukaryotic cells?
options: Prokaryotic cells are larger than eukaryotic cells and have more organelles inside
Eukaryotic cells lack ribosomes, so they must have evolved from simpler structures
Prokaryotic fossils are found only in the youngest layers of sedimentary rock
The oldest fossil cells are prokaryote-like, and eukaryote fossils appear much later
questions.explanation: Microfossils of simple prokaryote-like cells date back about 3.5 billion years, while fossils of eukaryotic cells appear well over a billion years later. Eukaryotic organelles also appear to be derived from prokaryotes. Prokaryotic cells are smaller and simpler, not larger.

questions.stem: What does the endosymbiotic theory propose about mitochondria and chloroplasts?
options: They are descended from prokaryotes taken in by an ancestral host cell
They formed from infoldings of the cell membrane of an early prokaryote
They are descended from viruses that infected an ancestral eukaryotic cell
They formed when the nucleus divided and part of it moved into the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: The theory proposes that free-living prokaryotes were engulfed by a host cell, survived inside it and became permanent organelles. Mitochondria probably came from aerobic bacteria and chloroplasts from photosynthetic cyanobacteria. Membrane infolding may explain other internal membranes, but not these organelles' own DNA and ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which feature of mitochondria is evidence for the endosymbiotic theory?
options: They are made by the nucleus whenever the cell needs extra energy supplies
They contain their own circular DNA and ribosomes like those of bacteria
They are found in the cytoplasm and are surrounded by the cell membrane
They make ATP using glucose that has been absorbed through the cell wall
questions.explanation: Mitochondria have circular DNA without histones and ribosomes like those of prokaryotes, they are about the size of bacteria, and they divide by a process like binary fission. A new mitochondrion only comes from an existing one, not from the nucleus.

questions.stem: Almost all eukaryotes have mitochondria, but only plants and algae have chloroplasts. What does this suggest about the endosymbiotic events?
options: Both organelles were taken in at once by a single photosynthetic host cell
Plants later lost their mitochondria when they gained their chloroplasts
The mitochondrial endosymbiosis happened first, before the chloroplast one
The chloroplast endosymbiosis happened first, before the mitochondrial one
questions.explanation: Because cells with chloroplasts also have mitochondria, but many cells with mitochondria have no chloroplasts, the mitochondrial event probably came first and a lineage of these cells later took in a cyanobacterium. Plant cells still have mitochondria and use them in cellular respiration.

questions.stem: Cytochrome c is a protein used in cellular respiration. Why is it useful for comparing species that are only distantly related?
options: It is made without DNA, so mutations never change its amino acid sequence
It is found in nearly all aerobic organisms and its sequence changes slowly
It is found only in mammals, so differences between mammals are very large
Its amino acid sequence is identical in every single species that has the protein
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c is part of the electron transport chain, so it is present in a very wide range of organisms. Its sequence changes slowly, so even distant species can be compared. Its sequence does differ between species, which is what allows the comparison.

questions.stem: The cytochrome c of four species is compared with that of humans. Species P differs at 0 amino acids, Q at 12, R at 21 and S at 44. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Species P and humans must be the same species, as the protein is identical
Species Q and R are more closely related to each other than to humans
Species P shares the most recent common ancestor with humans of the four
Species S shares the most recent common ancestor with humans of the four
questions.explanation: Fewer differences in a common protein mean less time for mutations to accumulate, so P separated from humans most recently. An identical protein does not make two organisms one species: humans and chimpanzees have identical cytochrome c. Differences from humans alone do not show how Q and R relate to each other.

questions.stem: In DNA-DNA hybridisation, how are single strands of DNA obtained from each species?
options: By cutting the DNA at recognition sites with a restriction enzyme
By copying one strand many times with the polymerase chain reaction
By translating the DNA into a chain of amino acids for comparison
By heating the DNA so the hydrogen bonds between strands break
questions.explanation: DNA from each species is heated to break the hydrogen bonds between bases, separating it into single strands. Single strands from the two species are then mixed and cooled so they pair to form hybrid DNA. Restriction enzymes and PCR are not part of this technique.

questions.stem: Hybrid DNA made from two species is reheated. Why does it separate at a lower temperature than DNA from a single species?
options: Hybrid DNA contains uracil instead of thymine, which makes the strands unstable
The two species' DNA is joined by covalent bonds, which are weaker than base pairs
Mismatched bases form fewer hydrogen bonds, so the hybrid is held less tightly
Hybrid DNA has extra hydrogen bonds, which break more easily when it is heated
questions.explanation: Where the base sequences differ, the bases cannot pair and form hydrogen bonds, so less energy is needed to separate the hybrid. The more differences there are, the lower the separation temperature. DNA does not contain uracil, and hydrogen bonds are weaker than covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Human DNA strands separate at 87.0 °C. Hybrid DNA of human and species W separates at 85.4 °C, human and X at 82.6 °C, and human and Y at 86.2 °C. Which species is most closely related to humans?
options: None, as hybrid DNA always separates at the same temperature
Species Y, as its hybrid separates closest to the human value
Species X, as its hybrid separates furthest from the human value
Species W, as its hybrid value lies midway between the other two
questions.explanation: The smaller the drop in separation temperature, the more bases are paired and the more similar the DNA sequences. Species Y drops only 0.8 °C, compared with 1.6 °C for W and 4.4 °C for X, so it is the closest relative. A large drop shows many mismatches and a more distant relationship.

questions.stem: Why are rRNA gene sequences widely used to work out the relationships between prokaryotes?
options: Prokaryotes have no other genes, so rRNA is the only DNA they contain
rRNA genes are found only in bacteria, so they separate them from archaea
rRNA genes change so quickly that every cell in a colony differs from others
All prokaryotes have rRNA genes, and parts of them change only slowly
questions.explanation: Every prokaryote needs ribosomes, so all have rRNA genes, and these contain slowly changing regions that allow even distantly related groups to be compared. Comparing rRNA gene sequences led to the recognition of archaea as a separate group from bacteria. Archaea also have rRNA genes.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, what does a branching point (node) represent?
options: A species that is still alive at the present day on Earth
A fossil that has been dated using radioactivity
A point at which two species merged into one
A common ancestor from which two lineages diverged
questions.explanation: Each node represents a common ancestor, where one lineage split into two. Living species are shown at the tips of the branches. Lineages diverge at nodes rather than merging.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, species A and B share a node, and that pair shares an older node with species C. Species D branches off from the base of the tree. Which statement is correct?
options: A is more closely related to C than it is to D
C is more closely related to A than it is to B
D is the ancestor of species A, B and C
A and B are less related than C and D are
questions.explanation: A and C share a common ancestor more recently than either shares with D, so A is closer to C than to D. C is equally related to A and B, because both connect to C through the same node. D is a living species at a tip, not an ancestor.

questions.stem: Why can mutations in DNA be used as a molecular clock?
options: Mutations accumulate over time, at a rate that can be estimated
Mutations happen only once each million years in every species
Mutations are removed from DNA at a fixed rate as an organism ages
Mutations occur only during the formation of fossils in rock
questions.explanation: If the rate at which differences accumulate in a DNA sequence is known, the number of differences between two species can be used to estimate how long ago they shared a common ancestor. The rate is estimated, often using fossils of known age.

questions.stem: Differences in a gene accumulate between two diverging lineages at about 4 base changes per million years. Two species differ at 24 bases in this gene. About when did they share a common ancestor?
options: About 96 million years ago
About 12 million years ago
About 3 million years ago
About 6 million years ago
questions.explanation: Time since divergence = number of differences / rate = 24 / 4 = 6 million years. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 96. The rate is given for the pair of lineages, so it should not be halved or doubled.

questions.stem: Why might a molecular clock based on one gene give an inaccurate divergence date?
options: The gene must have been identical in both species when they split
Mutations in a gene can only be counted in species that are extinct
A gene can only be compared between species living in one habitat
The mutation rate may not have stayed constant in every lineage
questions.explanation: A molecular clock assumes that differences accumulate at a steady, known rate, but rates can vary between genes, lineages and periods of time. Clocks are therefore calibrated against fossils of known age and checked with several genes. The gene was identical in the common ancestor, so that is not a source of error.

questions.stem: How is a species that reproduces sexually usually defined?
options: Members live in the same area and compete for the same food resources
Members look identical to each other and to their common ancestor
Members can mate with any similar species to produce living offspring
Members can actually or potentially interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: For sexually reproducing organisms, a species is a group whose members can interbreed, or could if they met, to produce fertile offspring. Living in one area does not make organisms one species, and producing living but sterile offspring, as horses and donkeys do, does not either.

questions.stem: Why can the interbreeding definition not be used to classify bacteria, and what is used instead?
options: Bacteria cannot be seen, so they are grouped by the habitat they live in
Bacteria have no DNA, so their shape is the only way to classify them
Bacteria all interbreed freely, so they are classed as a single species
Bacteria reproduce asexually, so biochemical and DNA similarity are used
questions.explanation: Organisms that reproduce asexually do not interbreed, so other criteria are used, such as biochemical similarity, morphological similarity and similarity of DNA sequences. Bacteria do have DNA, and rRNA gene sequences are widely used to classify them.

questions.stem: Male and female birds of one species look very different, while two other bird species look almost identical. What limitation of a species criterion does this show?
options: Biochemical similarity is always misleading for animal species
A common gene pool is only shared by organisms that look identical
Morphological similarity alone can wrongly group or split species
Interbreeding cannot be used for any animal that is able to fly
questions.explanation: Defining species by appearance can split one species whose males and females differ, or lump together separate species that look alike but do not interbreed. That is why biochemical similarity, a common gene pool and interbreeding are also used.

questions.stem: Two wattle species grow side by side in a South Australian reserve, but one flowers in winter and the other in late spring. Which isolating mechanism keeps them distinct?
options: Behavioural isolation
Mechanical isolation
Hybrid inviability
Temporal isolation
questions.explanation: Flowering at different times means pollen of one species is not available when the other is receptive, so no zygote forms. This is temporal isolation, a pre-zygotic mechanism. Hybrid inviability acts only after a zygote has formed, and behavioural isolation involves courtship signals between animals.

questions.stem: In two related species of firefly, males flash in different patterns, and females respond only to their own species' pattern. Which isolating mechanism is this?
options: Behavioural isolation
Temporal isolation
Gamete isolation
Hybrid sterility
questions.explanation: Different courtship signals mean the two species do not recognise each other as mates, so no zygote forms. This is behavioural isolation. Gamete isolation acts after mating, when sperm and egg cannot fuse.

questions.stem: Two coral species release eggs and sperm into the water on the same night. Their gametes mix, but very few eggs are fertilised by sperm of the other species. Which mechanism keeps the species distinct?
options: Mechanical isolation, as the two corals cannot physically join to mate
Gamete isolation, as sperm and egg of the two species cannot fuse
Temporal isolation, as the two species release gametes on one night
Hybrid sterility, as hybrids grow but cannot produce their own gametes
questions.explanation: The gametes meet but fail to fuse, usually because proteins on the egg and sperm surfaces do not match, so no zygote forms. This is gamete isolation, a pre-zygotic mechanism. Spawning on the same night rules out temporal isolation, and hybrid sterility acts only after a hybrid forms.

questions.stem: Eggs of one toad species fertilised by sperm of a related species begin to divide, but the embryos always die before hatching. Which isolating mechanism is this?
options: Hybrid inviability, a post-zygotic mechanism
Hybrid sterility, also a post-zygotic mechanism
Gamete isolation, a pre-zygotic mechanism
Temporal isolation, a pre-zygotic mechanism
questions.explanation: A zygote forms, so the barrier is post-zygotic, and the hybrid fails to develop, which is hybrid inviability. Hybrid sterility applies when hybrids develop and survive but cannot produce fertile offspring, as with the mule. Gamete isolation would stop fertilisation altogether.

questions.stem: Why is mutation described as the ultimate source of genetic variation?
options: It is the process that shuffles existing alleles
It always produces alleles that improve survival
It happens only in gametes during fertilisation
It is the process by which new alleles arise
questions.explanation: A mutation is a permanent change in the DNA nucleotide sequence, and it is how new alleles arise. Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation shuffle alleles that already exist. Most mutations are neutral or harmful rather than beneficial.

questions.stem: Which processes add genetic variation in a species that reproduces sexually, in addition to mutation?
options: Translation, transcription and the folding of proteins after synthesis
Natural selection, genetic drift and the extinction of small populations
Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation
Binary fission, mitosis and the replication of DNA before division
questions.explanation: During meiosis, crossing over and independent assortment produce gametes with new combinations of alleles, and random fertilisation combines gametes from two parents. Mitosis and binary fission produce genetically identical cells. Selection and drift change allele frequencies rather than creating variation.

questions.stem: Why will many mutations have no detectable effect on an organism?
options: They may occur in non-coding DNA or code for the same amino acid
They are always repaired before the cell can copy its DNA again
They change only the sugar of a nucleotide, not its nitrogen base
They affect only proteins, which cells can replace with new ones
questions.explanation: Much DNA does not code for proteins, and because the genetic code is degenerate, a base substitution can still code for the same amino acid. Recessive mutations may also be hidden by a dominant allele. Repair systems fix many errors, but not all, so mutations do persist.

questions.stem: People who are heterozygous for the sickle-cell allele are more resistant to malaria. Why is this allele more common in malaria-prone regions?
options: People in these regions choose partners who carry the sickle-cell allele
The allele is dominant there and recessive in regions without malaria
Heterozygotes survive malaria better and pass the allele to more offspring
Malaria infection causes the sickle-cell mutation to arise in each person
questions.explanation: In malaria-prone regions, heterozygotes are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the allele is passed on more often, even though two copies cause sickle-cell anaemia. Whether a mutation is beneficial depends on the selection pressure. Malaria does not cause the mutation.

questions.stem: What is a gene pool?
options: All the genes on one particular chromosome
All the species living in an ecosystem
All the genetic information in a population
All the alleles carried by a single organism
questions.explanation: A gene pool is the total of all the alleles carried by all the members of a population. A large gene pool with many alleles shows considerable genetic diversity, making the population more likely to survive selection pressures.

questions.stem: In a moth population, 20% of the alleles for wing colour code for dark wings. After soot darkens tree trunks, this rises to 70% over 50 generations. Which explanation is correct?
options: Moths changed their wing colour during their lives to match the dark trunks
The soot caused new dark-wing mutations in the moths that rested on trunks
The moths chose to become darker so the whole population would survive
Dark moths were eaten less often, so they left more offspring with the allele
questions.explanation: Dark moths were better camouflaged on sooty trunks, so birds ate fewer of them and they produced more offspring, raising the allele's frequency. Individuals do not change their alleles, and the population does not choose to adapt: the environment selects among existing variation.

questions.stem: A bushfire kills most of a small population of skinks at random, regardless of their traits. Afterwards some alleles have been lost entirely. What process is this?
options: Genetic drift
Natural selection
Gene flow
Mutation
questions.explanation: Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequencies, and its effects are strongest in small populations. Here survival had nothing to do with the skinks' traits, so it was not natural selection. Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of events in allopatric speciation?
options: Hybrid sterility, then geographical isolation, then the populations mix together again
Geographical isolation, then different selection and drift, then reproductive isolation
Reproductive isolation, then geographical isolation, then different selection pressures
Different selection pressures, then geographical isolation, then a single new mutation
questions.explanation: A geographical barrier first stops gene flow between populations. Different selection pressures, mutations and genetic drift then change each gene pool, until the populations can no longer interbreed even if they meet. Reproductive isolation is the result, not the starting point.

questions.stem: A river changes course and splits a population of flightless beetles. Thousands of years later, the two groups meet again but cannot produce fertile offspring. Which statement is correct?
options: They became two species at the moment the river first separated them
The beetles mutated on purpose so they could survive on each side
Their gene pools changed separately until they became reproductively isolated
They are still one species, because they share a recent common ancestor
questions.explanation: With no gene flow, different selection pressures and drift changed each gene pool until the groups could no longer produce fertile offspring, so they are now two species. Separation alone does not create species, and mutations are random rather than directed by need.

questions.stem: What is adaptive radiation?
options: The loss of genetic variation when a small group founds a new population
The divergent evolution of many species from one ancestor into different niches
The evolution of similar features in unrelated species in similar environments
The spread of a single species across a continent without any genetic change
questions.explanation: In adaptive radiation, one ancestral species gives rise to many species, each adapted to a different niche, as in Darwin's finches or Australian marsupials. Similar features in unrelated species is convergent evolution, and a small founding group losing variation is the founder effect.

questions.stem: The marsupial sugar glider and the placental flying squirrel both have a gliding membrane between their limbs, but they are not closely related. What does this show?
options: Divergent evolution from a recent shared ancestor
Adaptive radiation from a single gliding ancestor
Gene flow between the marsupials and the placentals
Convergent evolution under similar selection pressures
questions.explanation: Unrelated species living in similar environments face similar selection pressures, so they can evolve similar features independently, which is convergent evolution. Divergent evolution produces differences in related species. Marsupials and placentals cannot exchange genes.
